blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — SGLT2 inhibitor ketoacidosis recognition
stem: A client with type 2 diabetes who takes empagliflozin presents with nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and fatigue. Blood glucose is 210 mg/dL. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.A: Promptly assess for ketoacidosis, including ketones and acid-base status; empagliflozin-associated ketoacidosis can occur with glucose below 250 mg/dL.
options.B: Attribute the symptoms to volume depletion and defer ketoacidosis testing unless the glucose rises into a markedly hyperglycemic range.
options.C: Evaluate for hypoglycemia first and postpone acid-base testing because a glucose of 210 mg/dL does not fit empagliflozin-associated ketoacidosis.
options.D: Treat the symptoms as gastrointestinal intolerance and reassess later because ketoacidosis from empagliflozin is generally accompanied by marked hyperglycemia.

rationale: Current JARDIANCE labeling warns that diabetic ketoacidosis and other ketoacidosis can occur with SGLT2 inhibition even when blood glucose is below levels typically expected for DKA, including below 250 mg/dL. Compatible manifestations include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, malaise, dehydration, and shortness of breath, and the label directs clinicians to assess for ketoacidosis regardless of the presenting glucose level and promptly evaluate when suspected. Therefore A is the best answer. B incorrectly makes higher glucose a prerequisite for ketoacidosis evaluation. C is contradicted by the client's glucose and by the label's warning that SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis may occur without marked hyperglycemia. D incorrectly dismisses a potentially serious medication-related complication because the glucose is only modestly elevated.
educational_objective: Recognize that empagliflozin-associated ketoacidosis can present with only modest hyperglycemia; compatible symptoms warrant prompt assessment for ketones and metabolic acidosis regardless of the presenting glucose level.
source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine); source JARDIANCE label by Boehringer Ingelheim Pharmaceuticals, Inc.; repackaged by Cardinal Health 107, LLC
source_document_title: JARDIANCE (empagliflozin tablets), for oral use — Prescribing Information
source_locator: Full Prescribing Information §5.1 Diabetic Ketoacidosis in Patients with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus and Other Ketoacidosis: symptoms include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, generalized malaise, and shortness of breath; presenting glucose may be below typical DKA levels, e.g. <250 mg/dL; assess for ketoacidosis regardless of presenting blood glucose in clients with compatible symptoms and promptly evaluate if suspected.
source_claim_supported: Empagliflozin-associated ketoacidosis can occur with glucose below 250 mg/dL, so compatible symptoms warrant assessment for ketoacidosis regardless of presenting glucose.
blueprint_locator: Printed p. 38, Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: review pertinent data prior to medication administration; educate client about medications; evaluate client response to medication; assess for actual and potential medication side/adverse effects and intervene appropriately.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Removed the isolated absolute-word distractor pattern and converted the options into parallel clinical actions.
Reframed the stem around the nursing action required by the current warning while preserving the same SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis construct.
audit_note: Clinical content was re-audited from zero after revision. A directly follows the current §5.1 warning. B, C, and D each inappropriately delay or dismiss ketoacidosis assessment based on the glucose level. Volume depletion may coexist, but B is not defensible because it explicitly defers ketoacidosis evaluation. No second answer or material cueing remains.
